title: Stage 1 — Git & Collaboration
goal: Develop daily Git habits and learn to manage work with branches.
summary: Git for real work: the staging model, clean commits, branches, and a stage ← dev ← feature workflow.

checkpoint.prompt: A file you edited shows under "Changes not staged for commit". What does that mean?

choices.text: Git is tracking the file but the edit isn't in the next commit yet
The file is brand new and Git has never seen it
The change is already committed

checkpoint.explanation: Tracked-but-unstaged means Git knows the file but you haven't run `git add` on this change yet. Untracked is for brand-new files.

checkpoint.prompt: Which command stages only the file src/app.js (not everything)?
checkpoint.explanation: `git add src/app.js` stages just that file. `git add .` stages everything in the current directory — handy, but be intentional.

choices.text: feat: add email validation to signup form
stuff
fixed it finally

checkpoint.explanation: A good message names the change and its intent. "stuff" and "fixed it" tell a future reader (you!) nothing.

checkpoint.prompt: Which command creates a new branch called feature/login AND switches to it?
checkpoint.explanation: `git switch -c feature/login` (modern) or `git checkout -b feature/login` (classic) both create the branch and move you onto it in one step.

checkpoint.prompt: You finished feature/login. What's the typical next move in a team workflow?

choices.text: Push the branch and open a pull request to merge it into dev
Delete the branch and rewrite the code on main
Commit directly to main and skip review

checkpoint.explanation: Feature branches are pushed and merged via pull requests, which create a review point before code reaches shared branches.

checklist.label: A sensible project structure is committed
App runs locally (a minimal "hello" is fine)
Built something on a feature branch and merged it
At least one commit on a second, separate day

choices.text: Stages changes so they'll be included in the next commit
Pushes your commits to GitHub
Permanently deletes uncommitted changes

questions.explanation: `git add` moves changes into the staging area. `git push` sends commits to the remote.

questions.prompt: Git has three main areas a change moves through. What is the correct order?

choices.text: Working directory → staging area → repository
Repository → working directory → staging area
Staging area → repository → working directory

questions.explanation: You edit in the working directory, `git add` to staging, then `git commit` into the repository.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an acceptable daily commit on CommitLoop?

choices.text: feat: add workout list endpoint
An empty commit just to keep the streak
Bumping a timestamp in the README with no real change

questions.explanation: Commits should reflect real work: features, fixes, refactors, tests, docs, or structure.

choices.text: A movable pointer to a line of commits, letting you work in parallel
A separate copy of your files in another folder
A backup uploaded to GitHub

questions.explanation: A branch is just a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit. Switching branches changes which line of history you build on.

questions.prompt: Why build a feature on its own branch instead of directly on a shared branch?

choices.text: It isolates in-progress work so the shared branch stays stable and reviewable
Branches make your code run faster
You're required to delete shared branches afterward

questions.explanation: Feature branches keep unfinished work out of shared branches and give you a clean unit to review and merge.
